questions.title: The design tool's growth model
questions.prompt: You are the growth PM for a collaborative design tool with a free plan. Draw its growth model, find the constraint, and say where you would invest next quarter.
hints: How does one user bring in another?
Which step converts worst relative to its potential?
What turns a free team into a paying one?
followups: Invites are up but invited users rarely become active. What next?
Leadership wants paid acquisition doubled. Your view?
How would you know the loop is healthy, not just growing?
criteria: Describes a loop, not only a funnel (sharing a file brings in collaborators).
Quantifies steps and identifies the constraint.
Prioritises work on the constraint.
Connects to monetisation (team conversion).
Checks quality: retention of acquired users.
outline: Loop: user creates file → shares for feedback → collaborator views → signs up → creates own file.
Steps: share rate, view-to-signup, signup-to-active, team formation, paid conversion.
Constraint: e.g. invited viewers who never edit.
Bets: better viewer experience, commenting without sign-up, templates for new users.
Monetisation: team features at the point of collaboration.
Health: retention of loop-acquired users, paid conversion of teams.
questions.reference:
The core loop: a designer creates a file and shares it for feedback; collaborators open the link, comment, sign up and start their own files, which they share in turn. Paid conversion happens when a group starts working as a team and needs shared libraries and permissions.

I would measure each step — share rate per active user, viewers per share, viewer-to-signup, signup-to-first-file, team formation, paid conversion — and look for the weakest step relative to benchmarks or potential. Suppose many viewers open links but few sign up or create files: that is the constraint.

Next quarter I would invest there: let viewers comment without signing up, then ask them to sign up at the moment they want to do more; offer templates so a new user’s first file is easy; and show what collaborators can do on a team plan. Health checks: 30-day retention of users acquired through the loop and the share of new teams that convert to paid. Doubling paid acquisition makes sense only if those users retain as well as loop-acquired ones.
pitfalls: Optimising a step that is not the constraint.

questions.title: Sign-ups who never start
questions.prompt: Your budgeting app gets plenty of sign-ups, but most new users never connect a bank account, and those who do not connect leave within a week. Improve activation.
hints: Why might someone hesitate to connect a bank account?
Is connecting the right activation moment, or is it something after it?
Can users get value before connecting?
followups: Connection rate improves, but retention does not. What does that mean?
Which experiment would you run first?
How do you avoid pressuring users into sharing financial data?
criteria: Defines activation as the first real value, not a setup step.
Investigates reasons (trust, effort, bank coverage, errors) with data and research.
Proposes value before connection and trust-building.
Tests the biggest leak first.
Respects users; no dark patterns.
outline: Measure the funnel step by step; find errors in bank connection.
Research: interviews and session reviews with drop-offs.
Hypotheses: trust, failed connections, unclear benefit.
Ideas: manual budget first; show what they will see; clear security explanation; fix failing banks.
Activation = first insight (e.g. a spending summary) within a week.
Experiment and guardrails.
questions.reference:
First, measure the connection step precisely: how many start it, how many fail with technical errors (some banks have poor connections), and how many abandon. Then talk to people who dropped off.

Common reasons: they do not trust the app with bank access yet, the connection fails, or they do not see what they will get. Fixes match the reasons: let users start with a quick manual budget and see value before connecting; explain plainly what access means and what we cannot do; show a preview of the insights; and fix or flag banks with high failure rates.

I would define activation as receiving a first useful insight — a spending summary — within the first week, not as connecting. If connection rises but retention does not, the product after connection is the problem. The first experiment: a ‘start manually’ path versus the current flow, measured on week-four retention. No pressure tactics: users must feel safe choosing to share financial data.

questions.title: A winning test that may hurt
questions.prompt: A test that makes the 'cancel subscription' button harder to find reduced cancellations by 12% in two weeks. The team wants to ship it. What do you do?
hints: Who is not cancelling — satisfied users or frustrated ones?
What happens to complaints, chargebacks and reviews?
Are there rules about how easy cancellation must be?
followups: The CFO points to the revenue gain. Respond.
What test would you run instead?
How do you set growth guardrails for the team?
criteria: Recognises a dark pattern and its risks (trust, chargebacks, regulation).
Checks guardrails: complaints, refunds, support contacts, reviews.
Proposes ethical retention alternatives (pause, downgrade, address reasons).
Sets team-wide guardrails.
Communicates the decision with reasons.
outline: Do not ship: users who want to leave are being obstructed.
Check: support contacts, chargebacks, complaints, app-store reviews in treatment.
Regulatory and reputational risk.
Alternatives: cancellation survey with pause or downgrade options; fix top cancellation reasons.
Guardrails for all growth tests: complaint rate, chargebacks, long-term retention.
questions.reference:
I would not ship it. Making cancellation harder does not create value; it delays users who have already decided to leave. The cost shows up elsewhere: support contacts, chargebacks when people dispute charges with their bank, complaints and reviews, and regulatory risk in places that require easy cancellation. I would check those numbers in the treatment group — they usually rise.

Instead, I would test honest retention: at cancellation, ask why, and offer what fits — pause the subscription, switch to a cheaper plan, or fix a problem — with cancelling still one clear step away. And I would invest in the top cancellation reasons.

To the CFO: the two-week gain is likely borrowed from future trust and chargebacks. I would also set team guardrails for every growth test: complaint rate, refunds and chargebacks, and 90-day retention, so a ‘win’ that harms users cannot ship.

questions.title: Retention that never flattens
questions.prompt: Your language-learning app's retention curve keeps declining and never flattens: most users are gone within two months. What do you do?
hints: What does a flattening curve mean, and which users flatten?
Which early behaviours predict users who stay?
Is the problem habit, value or difficulty?
followups: Notifications increase day-7 retention but not day-60. Why?
Users who join a class retain much better. Is that a lever?
How do you measure long-term value of a change quickly?
criteria: Analyses curves by cohort and segment to find any that flatten.
Finds behaviours associated with retention and tests causality.
Distinguishes habit from real progress.
Proposes changes to core value, not just reminders.
Uses leading indicators validated against long-term retention.
outline: Segment curves: goal, level, channel; find flattening segments.
Behaviours of retained users: streaks, classes, real-life use.
Causality: experiments, not correlation.
Ideas: visible progress toward real goals; social commitment; adaptive difficulty.
Leading indicator validated against day-60.
questions.reference:
A curve that never flattens means no group has found lasting value yet. I would segment retention by goal (travel, work, school), starting level and acquisition channel to see whether any group flattens — that group shows what working looks like.

Then look at early behaviours of users who stay: maybe they join a live class, set a concrete goal or reach a milestone such as a first real conversation. Those are hypotheses, not levers: committed people may simply do more of everything. I would test causally — for example, invite a random half of new users to a class.

Notifications lift short-term return but not long-term retention because they create habit without value. Changes to the core experience matter more: visible progress toward the user’s real goal, adaptive difficulty, and commitment with others. To move quickly, I would validate a leading indicator — say, week-two progress — against day-60 retention, then use it in experiments.

questions.title: Free plan too generous?
questions.prompt: Your note-taking app's free plan is so generous that only 2% of active users pay. Leadership wants more paying users without losing the free growth engine. What do you propose?
hints: Which free users get the most value — and would pay?
What is the value metric that should separate free from paid?
How do you change a free plan without angering existing users?
followups: How would you test willingness to pay?
Existing free users are upset. How do you handle it?
How do you know you have not damaged acquisition?
criteria: Segments users by value and willingness to pay.
Chooses a value metric aligned with heavy, professional use.
Moves paywalls to moments of high value, keeps the free engine intact.
Tests pricing and packaging before rollout.
Grandfathers or communicates changes carefully; watches acquisition.
outline: Segment: casual, heavy individual, team/professional.
Value metric: devices synced, storage, collaboration, advanced search.
Package: keep core free; move professional features to paid.
Test: price tests, fake-door tests, surveys.
Rollout: new users first; grandfather existing; clear communication.
Guardrails: sign-ups, activation, referrals.
questions.reference:
I would start by segmenting active free users: casual note-takers, heavy individual users and people using the app for work or in teams. The heavy and professional segments get the most value and are the likely payers.

Then choose what separates free from paid. A good value metric grows with how much someone relies on the product — syncing across many devices, large storage, collaboration, advanced search — so casual users stay free and the growth engine keeps working, while heavy users meet the paywall at a moment of real value.

Before changing anything, test willingness to pay: price tests on new users, a fake-door test for a professional tier, and interviews. Roll out to new users first and keep existing users’ current features for a period, with clear communication. Guardrails: sign-ups, activation and referrals must not fall; I would also track paid conversion by segment and 90-day retention of payers.

questions.title: Growth you said no to
questions.prompt: Tell me about a growth opportunity you decided not to pursue, or a winning experiment you chose not to ship. Why?
followups: Was it the right call in hindsight?
What principle did you take from it?
criteria: Real tension between short-term numbers and users or long-term value.
Evidence-based reasoning.
Persuaded stakeholders.
Outcome known.
Principle stated.
outline: Opportunity and its apparent value.
Concern.
Evidence gathered.
Decision and persuasion.
Outcome.
Principle.
questions.reference: A strong answer (a model of structure, not a script): “An experiment that auto-enrolled users in weekly marketing emails raised return visits 6%. Unsubscribes and spam reports tripled, which threatened our email deliverability for transactional messages. I showed the team the deliverability risk and proposed an opt-in version with a clear benefit; it recovered about half the lift without the complaints. My principle: a growth win has to survive a look at its guardrails.”
pitfalls: A story with no real cost.
